newsitem.title: USA: LTV Corp chief "bullish" despite union strife.
newsitem.headline: LTV Corp chief "bullish" despite union strife.

text.p: LTV Corp chairman David Hoag told Reuters the company was still bullish on 1997, but he declined to comment on analysts' earnings projections of $1.01 for the year.
Earnings for the steel company's first quarter, announced just before the annual shareholder meeting Thursday, were $0.25 a share, slightly ahead of a projected $0.24.
Company directors were not at the meeting, but Hoag said they will consider a dividend on Friday when they meet at company headquarters in Cleveland.

Hoag said 826,000 shares of common stock have been bought back so far under a $75 million repurchase plan begun in January. But despite the company's $653.0 million in cash and marketable securities and $307.2 million in credit facilities, another plan will not be considered any time soon.

"We do need to grow this company. We need cash for a strong liquidity position in a downturn and cash for acquisitions...We look at possible acquisitions (overseas) as well as domestic," Hoag said, adding the company intended to expand its core flat-rolled steel business, as well as add related businesses upstream and downstream.
"We're doing very well in the competitive battle with aluminum and plastic," Hoag said.

He forecast a new market for steel in the residential industry where he expected the strength and consistent pricing of steel to attract builders concerned about price fluctuations and supply problems of wood.

At the sparsely-attended meeting in the Hotel duPont, Hoag fielded questions for three hours from a delegation of 40 Cleveland Works employees, all members of the United Steel Workers of America, who came by chartered bus.

They criticized "undeserved" executive compensation, the failure of directors to attend the annual meeting two years in a row, LTV's alleged plan to "create a union-free environment in this country" and allegedly unsafe plant conditions, which they said caused the deaths of four workers in the past year.

National USWA officer Leo Gerard said workers felt betrayed by management when it opened the non-union mini-mill Trico Steel, in Decatur, Alabama, a 50 percent joint venture with Sumitomo Steel and British Steel whose products compete with the Cleveland Works.
In other business, a slate of four directors was elected and a management incentive plan was approved.
